strengths: Addresses a practically important problem for deploying MLLM-based embedders: the quadratic cost of dense visual token sequences, which is often overlooked by prior work focused solely on discriminative performance.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning MMEB (36 sub-datasets), visual document retrieval (VisDoc), and cross-modal retrieval (Flickr30K, MSCOCO, ShareGPT4V, Urban1K, SugarCrepe), with consistent state-of-the-art results at both 2B and 8B scales.
Strong efficiency gains are clearly quantified (e.g., latency reduced from 162.8ms to 29.9ms vs. LLaVE-2B, visual tokens reduced by 75%), directly supporting the paper's efficiency claims.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each pipeline stage (warm-up, global hard negative mining, MLLM-judge fine-tuning, reranker), the number/type of hard negatives, LoRA rank, and training-time benefits of token compression, providing good insight into what drives the gains.
Reasonably detailed description of datasets, templates, and hyperparameters (including appendix tables) aids reproducibility for the parts based on public data.

The 'retrieve-and-judge' MLLM-as-a-judge strategy for both hard-negative mining and expanding true positives is a sensible, well-motivated engineering solution to the false-negative problem in contrastive training.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: the core architectural contribution (bilinear interpolation for visual token compression) is an existing technique borrowed directly from cited prior work (LLaVA-OneVision/LLaVA-NeXT), not a new method; the paper's main contribution is a careful combination and scaling of known techniques (compression + hard-negative mining + MLLM-as-judge) rather than a novel algorithmic idea.

Many components of the training pipeline (multi-stage progressive training, hard negative mining, MLLM-as-a-judge for data curation, reranker synergy) are conceptually very close to prior works already cited (e.g., UniME-V2, GME, LamRA), making the incremental contribution somewhat unclear beyond re-engineering these ideas around a compressed backbone.

Heavy reliance on large-scale in-house/proprietary data (e.g., in-house captioning and classification data in Stage 1) reduces full reproducibility of the reported results, despite otherwise good documentation of public datasets.

The compression ratio ablation is limited to a single setting (factor of 2 spatially, i.e., 4x token reduction); there is no exploration of the efficiency-performance trade-off curve across different compression ratios, nor a comparison against learned/alternative compression schemes (e.g., resamplers, Q-formers) that the paper claims are inferior but never empirically tests.

Cross-backbone comparisons (InternVL3-VTC vs. Qwen2VL, LLaVA-OV-based baselines) confound architecture, pretraining corpus, and training strategy differences, making it difficult to cleanly attribute gains to the proposed compression/training pipeline versus backbone-specific factors.

No analysis of the reliability/accuracy of the MLLM-judge itself (e.g., agreement with human labels, sensitivity to judge model choice), which is central to the Stage 3 data curation and reranker training.

The overall training pipeline is highly resource-intensive (48× A800 GPUs, tens of millions of samples across three stages), which may limit practical reproducibility and broader adoption despite the efficiency gains claimed at inference time.
Minor writing/grammar issues throughout (e.g., 'enhance the model for handle diverse scenarios') suggest the manuscript would benefit from a careful proofreading pass.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical validation across three complementary benchmark families (MMEB natural-image retrieval, VisDoc visual-document retrieval, and cross-modal retrieval on Flickr30K/MSCOCO/ShareGPT4V/Urban1K/SugarCrepe), with consistent state-of-the-art results at both 2B and 8B scale.

Strong efficiency-performance trade-off is convincingly demonstrated: the method achieves SOTA accuracy while using roughly 1/4 to 1/70 of the visual tokens compared to competing MLLM embedders, with corresponding wall-clock latency reductions measured on real hardware (Table 6).

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each pipeline stage (contrastive warm-up, global hard-negative mining, MLLM-judge fine-tuning, reranker), the number/type of hard negatives, the effect of token compression on training efficiency, and LoRA rank — providing good insight into what drives the gains.

The three-stage training recipe (generative restoration → contrastive pretraining with hard-negative mining → MLLM-as-judge task-aware finetuning) is a sensible and well-motivated way to compensate for potential information loss from aggressive token compression, and the paper shows this recipe is necessary (naive contrastive training on the compressed backbone alone is insufficient).
Detailed reporting of datasets, templates, and hyperparameters (appendices) aids reproducibility for the parts built on public data.

The synergistic reranker, trained on the same judge-curated data as the embedder, is a nice touch that meaningfully improves two-stage retrieval performance without introducing an independent data source.
weaknesses: The core architectural contribution (parameter-free bilinear interpolation for token compression) is not new — it is directly adapted from existing work (LLaVA-Next/InternVL-style downsampling, cited as [44,103]) rather than a novel compression mechanism; the paper does not compare against alternative compression strategies (e.g., token merging, learned pooling/query-based abstractors, attention-based pruning) to justify why simple interpolation is preferable beyond the general appeal to avoiding optimization difficulty.

Most individual training-pipeline components (hard-negative mining, MLLM-as-a-judge data curation, multi-stage progressive training, joint pointwise/listwise reranker training) already exist in prior work (e.g., UniME-V2, LamRA, GME); the paper's contribution is primarily a careful combination/engineering integration of known techniques with a compressed backbone, rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea. This should be judged as an applied/systems contribution, which is reasonable, but the novelty claims in the introduction slightly overstate the conceptual originality.

Significant reliance on large-scale in-house/proprietary data (e.g., ShareGPT4V captioning augmentation and classification data in Stage 1, Table 1) limits full reproducibility of the reported results, even though most other components use public datasets.

The compression ratio is fixed at a single setting (spatial downsampling by 2, i.e., 75% token reduction); no exploration of the accuracy-efficiency trade-off curve across multiple compression ratios is provided, which would strengthen the central claim that this is a well-chosen operating point rather than an arbitrary one.

Latency benchmarking uses batch size 1 on a single GPU without production-style batched throughput comparisons or acceleration techniques (the paper acknowledges prefix caching could change conclusions for VisDoc query latency), which somewhat limits the practical generalizability of the efficiency claims to real deployment scenarios.

The judge model (Qwen3-VL) used for hard-negative curation and relevance re-labeling is from the same model family as some comparison points in related literature (e.g., Qwen3-VL-Embedding), raising a mild concern about potential distillation-style advantage or evaluation circularity that is not discussed.
Minor writing/grammar issues throughout (e.g., 'constrastive', 'training triplets', 'traing') that should be corrected in a final version but do not affect the scientific content.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored bottleneck (visual token redundancy) in MLLM-based multimodal embedding models, which is a legitimate and timely efficiency concern for deployment.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three benchmark families (MMEB natural image retrieval, VisDoc visual document retrieval, and cross-modal retrieval on Flickr30K/MSCOCO/ShareGPT4V/Urban1K/SugarCrepe), with both embedder-only and embedder+reranker settings reported.

Strong quantitative results: the method achieves new SOTA numbers at both 2B and 8B scale while using only ~64 visual tokens (25% of baseline), with clear latency/throughput measurements (including vLLM deployment under concurrent load) substantiating the efficiency claims.

Extensive and informative ablations: number of visual tokens vs. performance/computation trade-off, choice of compression operator (bilinear interpolation vs Conv2d vs AdaptiveAvgPool2d), LoRA rank, number/type of hard negatives, robustness to judge model choice (Qwen3-VL vs InternVL3), and stage-wise contribution analysis (Table 5) that clearly demonstrate the necessity of each of the three training stages.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility information: training data composition, per-dataset instructions, hyperparameters, and prompt templates are provided in the appendix, aiding replication despite lack of an explicit code/checkpoint release statement.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the token compression module (bilinear interpolation + pixel unshuffle) is a straightforward reuse of existing InternVL-style spatial downsampling, and the three-stage training pipeline (generative restoration → contrastive pretraining with hard negatives → MLLM-as-judge fine-tuning) closely mirrors concurrent works (e.g., UniME-V2, GME, LamRA) cited in the paper; the contribution is largely an engineering combination/systematic application rather than a new algorithmic idea.

Backbone confound in comparisons: SOTA claims versus baselines (e.g., UniME-V2 on Qwen2-VL/LLaVA-OV, GME on Qwen2-VL) are made across different underlying MLLM backbones (InternVL3-VTC vs Qwen2-VL/LLaVA-OV), making it difficult to cleanly attribute gains to the proposed compression+training pipeline versus backbone differences; a controlled same-backbone ablation against at least one strong baseline method would strengthen the causal claims.

The efficiency accounting in Stage 3 excludes the substantial extra inference cost of running the Qwen3-VL-8B judge model over training data for hard-negative/positive discovery; while this is a one-time offline training cost, it is not discussed as an added resource requirement relative to baselines that do not use such curation.

Potential data overlap/optimistic evaluation setup: Stage 3 fine-tuning and final evaluation both use MMEB-train/MMEB and Colpali-train/VisRAG splits, which is standard practice in the field but is not explicitly flagged as an in-domain train/eval relationship, and out-of-distribution generalization (OOD columns) is comparatively less impressive than in-domain gains in several tables.

No explicit discussion of limitations or failure cases (e.g., where the compressed 64-token representation clearly underperforms, particularly fine-grained OCR-heavy visual document scenarios) despite the paper itself noting GME outperforms the standalone embedder on VisDoc; a deeper analysis of when compression hurts would improve scientific completeness.

The paper does not clarify whether code, model weights, or training data (particularly the 5.8M in-house Stage 1 data and in-house classification data) will be released, which affects full reproducibility of the reported results.

strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored bottleneck (visual token redundancy) in MLLM-based multimodal embedding models, combining architectural efficiency with training strategy design in a coherent framework.

Strong empirical results: the proposed model achieves new SOTA on MMEB, VisDoc, and multiple cross-modal retrieval benchmarks while using only ~25% of the visual tokens of comparable baselines, demonstrating that efficiency and effectiveness need not trade off.

Extensive and well-designed ablation studies covering the choice of compression method (bilinear interpolation vs. conv/pooling), sensitivity to number of visual tokens, contribution of each training stage, number/type of hard negatives, judge model choice, and LoRA rank—these substantially strengthen the empirical case and aid understanding of what drives performance.

Thorough efficiency evaluation, including per-query/candidate latency, throughput under concurrent load with vLLM deployment, and training-time comparisons, giving a realistic picture of deployment benefits.

Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, prompt/input templates, dataset compositions, and task instructions are provided in appendices, which would facilitate replication of most components (aside from proprietary in-house data).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: parameter-free bilinear interpolation + pixel unshuffle for token compression is largely adapted from existing InternVL/Qwen-style pipelines, and several training ingredients (progressive multi-stage training, MLLM-as-a-judge hard negative mining, hard negative gradient/mining strategies, embedder+reranker synergy) closely mirror techniques already proposed in cited prior works (e.g., UniME-V2, LamRA, various hard-negative mining papers); the contribution is primarily a careful, effective combination and systematic study rather than a fundamentally new method.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully controlled for data scale/composition (e.g., the paper itself notes GME's advantage stems from proprietary training data), making it harder to cleanly attribute performance gains to the proposed architecture/training strategy versus data differences.

The visual token count ablation (Fig. 3, Table S4) is only conducted at the 2B scale; it is unclear whether the same compression ratio and performance trade-off generalize to the 8B model, which limits the generality of the core token-efficiency claim.

A portion of the training data (5.8M instruction-tuning samples and 2.8M classification samples) is proprietary in-house data, which limits full reproducibility of stage 1 training despite otherwise detailed documentation.

Limited analysis of failure modes or qualitative error cases for the compression module or the MLLM-judge-curated negatives/positives (e.g., how often judge errors propagate into training, or where compression degrades fine-grained retrieval), which would help calibrate confidence in the robustness of the pipeline.
